In node2vec, reusing samples along random walks of length l > k means that a longer walk can generate multiple overlapping training contexts, so the same sampled walk segment contributes to several neighborhood pairs. The main benefit is computational efficiency: compared with performing separate pure breadth-first search (BFS) or depth-first search (DFS) explorations for each context, node2vec amortizes sampling cost across many training examples. In practice, this reduces the number of independent traversals needed and lowers the effective time complexity of neighborhood sampling, because one random walk can be reused to produce multiple skip-gram-style co-occurrence pairs.

From a space perspective, the reuse strategy is also favorable because node2vec does not need to materialize full BFS/DFS trees or store all explored frontier states for each source node. Instead, it only needs to keep the current walk state and the generated samples, so memory usage is closer to linear in the walk length and the number of sampled contexts rather than exponential in branching factor as in explicit tree expansion.

Relative to pure BFS, node2vec avoids the high frontier growth that can occur when exploring all nodes at a given radius. Relative to pure DFS, it avoids repeatedly deep-expanding separate paths for each context. The tradeoff is that node2vec provides approximate neighborhood sampling rather than exhaustive search, but that approximation is what enables the efficiency gains. So the key complexity advantage is lower time and space cost per training sample through sample reuse along longer random walks, not exact graph traversal.
